title: Binary Search Tree: Lowest Common Ancestor
directAnswer: Exploit the BST ordering: start at the root and compare both target values to the current node. If both are smaller, the LCA is in the left subtree; if both are larger, it's in the right. The first node where the two targets fall on different sides (or one equals the node) is the lowest common ancestor — that's the split point. It runs in O(h) time and O(1) space, with no extra path storage. The general-binary-tree LCA is O(n); here the BST property makes it a guided descent.

remember.pattern: Guided BST descent until the two targets split
rules: Both targets **smaller** → go left; both **larger** → go right.
The **split point** (targets diverge, or one equals the node) is the LCA — return it immediately.
Works because a BST sorts values left-to-right, so the LCA is the last shared step of two searches.
O(h) time, **O(1) space** — no need to store root-to-node paths like the general-tree solution.
A node is an ancestor of itself, so if one target IS an ancestor of the other, that node is the LCA.
whenToUse: LCA when the tree is a BST (ordering lets you skip the O(n) search)
Finding the split point of two BST search paths
Range/interval queries that pivot on where two keys diverge
antiSignals: The tree is NOT a BST → general LCA recursion (search both subtrees), O(n)
Many repeated LCA queries on a static tree → preprocess with binary lifting / Euler tour + RMQ
Targets may be absent → add an existence check; plain descent assumes both are present
remember.takeaway: On a BST, LCA is the point where two downward searches part ways. Comparing both targets to each node turns an O(n) tree search into an O(h) guided walk with no extra memory — the cleanest payoff of the sorted-tree property.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the BST ordering to find the LCA in O(h) without storing paths, rather than running the general O(n) tree algorithm.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using the generic LCA (searching both subtrees) and ignoring the BST property, or mishandling the case where one target equals the current node (it should be the LCA).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that the LCA is the split point of two BST searches, derive the three-way comparison, and note the O(1) space win over the general-tree path-storing approach.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary search tree and two node values `v1` and `v2`, return the **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of the two nodes — the deepest node that has both `v1` and `v2` as descendants (a node is a descendant of itself).

You may assume both values exist in the tree.
constraints: All node values are unique (it is a valid BST)
Both v1 and v2 are guaranteed to be present in the tree
understanding: The LCA of two nodes is the deepest node from which one target lies in (or is) the left subtree and the other in (or is) the right subtree — the point where their two root-to-node paths diverge. In a BST, the sorted ordering tells us which way each search would go, so we can walk straight to that divergence point.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree guaranteed to be a BST?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point. The ordering lets us pick a direction at each node instead of searching both subtrees, dropping the cost from O(n) to O(h).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can one node be an ancestor of the other?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A node is its own ancestor, so if v1 is an ancestor of v2, the LCA is v1 — handled naturally because one target equals the current node at the split.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are both values guaranteed to exist?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem assumes so. If they might be absent, add a search to confirm presence first, since plain descent would otherwise return a node that isn't a true common ancestor.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the node or its value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return the node (pointer). HackerRank's signature returns the node; print or read its value as needed.

examples.explanation: 2 < 6 and 8 > 6 — they split at the root, so the LCA is 6.
Both < 6 → go left to 2; both > 2 → go right to 4; 3 < 4 and 5 > 4 → split at 4.
4 > 6? no, both < 6 → left to 2. Now one target IS 2 → 2 is an ancestor of 4, so LCA = 2.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Store Both Root-to-Node Paths
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the general-tree fallback that ignores the BST property — then show the ordering lets you skip the path storage.
hints: Forget the ordering for a moment: how would you find the LCA in ANY binary tree given two node values?
Record the path from the root to each target as a list of nodes.
Walk both paths in parallel from the root; the last node they share is the LCA.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building each path may visit up to O(n) nodes (in a general search) and the paths take O(n) space; comparing them is O(h). Total O(n) time and O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the approach that works for *any* binary tree, BST or not, and it's worth stating to show you know the general technique before specializing.

**Find the two paths.** Compute the list of nodes from the root down to `v1`, and separately from the root down to `v2`. In a general tree this means a search; in a BST you could use the ordering, but the brute-force framing assumes you don't.

**Compare the paths.** Both paths start at the root and share a common prefix. Walk them in lockstep while the nodes match; the *last* matching node before they diverge is the lowest common ancestor. Everything after that point goes into different subtrees.

**Why we can do better on a BST.** Storing two full paths costs O(n) memory, and you make two separate descents. The BST ordering lets you do a *single* descent and detect the divergence on the fly — no path lists, O(1) space. That's the optimization the next approach captures.
approaches.insight: The LCA is, by definition, the last shared node of two root-to-target paths. Seeing it that way makes the BST optimization obvious: we don't need to store the paths if the ordering tells us, at each step, whether the two paths still agree on a direction.

approaches.name: BST Guided Descent — Split Point (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. One descent, O(1) space, using the ordering.
hints: At the root, where would a BST search for v1 go? Where would a search for v2 go? When do those two searches first take different turns?
If both targets are less than the current node, both searches go left; if both are greater, both go right.
The first node where the targets fall on opposite sides — or where one equals the node — is the LCA. Return it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: You descend a single root-to-LCA path doing O(1) comparison per level → O(h) time. Only a single pointer is kept → O(1) space (no recursion, no path lists).
approaches.explanation:
In a BST, searching for a value is a sequence of left/right turns dictated by comparisons. The LCA of two values is precisely the node at which their two searches *first diverge*.

**The three cases at each node.** Compare both targets `a` and `b` against the current node's value:

1. **Both smaller** (`a < node` and `b < node`): both searches turn left, so the LCA must be deeper on the left — move to `node.left`.
2. **Both larger** (`a > node` and `b > node`): both turn right — move to `node.right`.
3. **Otherwise** (one is ≤ and the other is ≥, i.e. they split, or one equals the node): the two searches part ways here — this node is the LCA, so return it.

**Why the split point is the answer.** Up to this node, both targets shared every turn, meaning both live in the same subtree at each step — this node is a common ancestor. The moment they diverge, one target is in the left subtree (or is this node) and the other in the right (or is this node), so no deeper node can be ancestor to *both*. Hence this is the *lowest* common ancestor.

**Ancestor-of-itself case.** If one target equals the current node, case 3 fires (it's neither strictly-both-less nor strictly-both-greater), and we correctly return that node — matching the rule that a node is its own ancestor.

**Why O(1) space.** Unlike the brute force, we never store the paths; we detect divergence as we walk, keeping just one pointer. The descent stops at the LCA, never going below it.
approaches.insight: LCA on a BST = 'walk down until the two keys want to go different directions.' The sorted property converts a two-subtree search into a single guided descent — the canonical example of letting structure replace search.

elif v1 > node.data and v2 > node.data: node = node.right

pitfalls: Using strict < on one side and <= on the other inconsistently — breaks the ancestor-of-itself case.
Recursing into both subtrees like the general-tree LCA — wastes the BST property.
Assuming targets exist without checking when the problem doesn't guarantee it.

commonMistakes: Running the general O(n) two-subtree LCA instead of using the BST ordering.
Mishandling the case where one target is an ancestor of the other.
Storing full paths (O(n) space) when an O(1) descent suffices.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the BST property
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The generic LCA searches both subtrees at every node, costing O(n). On a BST the ordering tells you which single direction to take, so you should descend, not search.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Breaking the ancestor-of-itself case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If one target equals the current node, that node IS the LCA. Using strict-both-less / strict-both-greater leaves equality to fall into the else branch correctly; mixing in <= can skip past the true LCA.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if v1 <= node.data and v2 <= node.data:   # <= can descend past an equal target
    node = node.left
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if v1 < node.data and v2 < node.data:      # strict: equal target triggers the split
    node = node.left

patternNote: Guided BST descent to a split point. Because a BST orders values left-to-right, the LCA of two keys is the first node where their searches diverge — found in a single O(h), O(1)-space walk. This is the structure-replaces-search payoff; the general (non-BST) LCA must search both subtrees in O(n).
